summary:
## The Medusa Concept: A Tale of Two Companies

The **Dreadbox/Polyend Medusa** is a 2018 hybrid synthesizer, sequencer, and controller. It represents a unique collaboration between **Dreadbox**, known for modern analog circuits, and **Polyend**, celebrated for innovative digital sequencers. The synth combines the distinct philosophies of both European companies into a single, complex instrument.

## Sound Engine: Analog Meets Digital
Medusa features a dual-personality sound engine with six oscillators in total.

### Analog Section (Dreadbox)
*   **3 Analog Oscillators**: Forms the warm, "Greek goodness" core of the synth.
*   Features include **hard sync** between oscillator pairs, **FM** (Osc 3 modulating Osc 1 & 2), and **filter FM**.
*   Paired with a classic Dreadbox analog **filter**.

> [!NOTE]
The synth can sometimes be slightly out of tune, reducing the need for aggressive detuning.

### Digital Section (Polyend)
*   **3 Digital Oscillators**: Can function as standard digital oscillators or use **wavetables**.
*   **64 Wavetables**: A single table is selected at a time, with modulation of the wave position available per-oscillator. Sounds range from "cold chords" to "throaty abominations."
*   **Adjustable Noise Generator**: Color can be swept from "brown" to "annoying" (white/blue).

## Modulation & Voicing
*   **LFOs**: Multiple variable-waveform LFOs can be assigned directly to parameters without a traditional mod matrix.
*   **Envelopes**: 5-stage envelopes that can be looped.
*   **Voicing Modes**:
    *   **Monophonic**: A 6-oscillator "mono monster."
    *   **Paraphonic**: Two distinct 3-voice paraphonic modes.
    *   **FM Mode**: A 3-operator FM synth mode was added in a later firmware update.

## The Grid: Controller & Sequencer
The 64-pad grid is the central nervous system of the Medusa.

### Play Mode
*   Acts as an expressive controller with various **scales** and layouts.
*   Transmits **aftertouch**.
*   Generates additional modulation data based on where a pad is pressed and held, similar to MPE.

### Sequencer Mode
*   Powerful step sequencer with up to **8 bars** per pattern.
*   **Parameter Locks**: The standout feature. Over 100 parameters can be automated per step, effectively allowing a different patch on each step of the sequence.
*   Features include swing, a randomizer, and variable playback directions.

> [!TIP]
Parameter locks are a core part of Medusa's intended workflow, allowing for incredibly complex and evolving sequences that blend its analog and digital sounds.

## Drawbacks and Quirks
*   **Hardware Feel**: Knobs and faders can feel wobbly.
*   **User Interface**: Many essential parameters are hidden in menus. The monochrome pads lack the clarity of a multi-color system.
*   **Connectivity**: Features a full MIDI trio (In/Out/Thru) but only a **single mono audio output**.
*   **Discontinuation**: The Medusa was discontinued in 2021.

## Final Verdict
Medusa is described as a "strange beast" where the two halves—Dreadbox's analog and Polyend's digital—don't always communicate flawlessly. 

*   **Strengths**: A powerful and innovative toolbox for experienced sound designers who can leverage its versatile sequencer, deep modulation, and unique parameter lock system. It truly shines when combined with external effects.
*   **Weaknesses**: For musicians seeking conventional synth tones (e.g., "Moog-ish beefiness"), it can be frustrating and may lack the expected punch and sophistication.

> [!IMPORTANT]
This instrument is more of a complex sound design workstation than a simple plug-and-play synthesizer. Its true power is unlocked by embracing its unique, sequencer-driven workflow.
transcription:
## A Polish-Greek Collaboration

Welcome to Bad Gear, the show about the world's most hated audio tools. Synth history was shaped by Japanese and American manufacturers. Sure, there are some vintage gems from the old continent, but most of the archetypal designs have their origin in the Land of the Rising Sun.

Today we are going to talk about Medusa. This 2018 hybrid synthesizer, sequencer, and controller was designed by two companies that, among others, helped turn Europe into the center of innovation and swag in the field of electronic musical instruments. While Dreadbox is known for their modern takes on classic analog circuitry, Polyend (they sent this unit over as a long-term loan) has a history of bringing hardware sequencer concepts to the 21st century.

So this one's gotta be good. This one's gotta be good, right?

## Analog and Digital Sound Engines

At the first glance, the monstrous mortal daughter of Phorcys and Ceto is ticking all the boxes. A Janus-faced concept based on analog Dreadbox oscillators and filters which are so hot right now. Massive metal enclosure, plenty of hands-on controls, but it's never enough, and I'm pretty sure no one's complaining about a lack of LFOs.

All the analog Greek goodness is controlled digitally, and Polyend added three digital oscillators with wavetables. You can select only one of the 64 wavetables at a time, but the position can be modulated independently for each oscillator. The collection of waveforms ranges from cold-sounding chords to throaty abominations, and depending on the table in use, tweaking can be either smooth or steppy. There is aliasing in the higher octaves. Brightness of the noise generator can be adjusted from brown to annoying.

## Modulation and Voicing Modes

The analog oscillator section has a few more tricks up its sleeve: hard sync between oscillator pairs, FM of the first two oscillators with oscillator 3 being used as the modulator, and tasty filter FM.

I never felt the need to detune the oscillators, as the synth is slightly out of tune most of the time anyway. Medusa comes without a modulation matrix. Just select a target for the variable waveform LFOs and loopable but not super punchy 5-stage envelopes. Dial in the desired amount and you're good to go. Modulating pulse width gives us yet another excuse for a Nik-Batt meme riff. The synth can be used as a 6-oscillator mono monster.

There are two paraphonic modes, and the latest firmware added 3-op FM.

## The Grid: Controller and Sequencer

This epic depth of parameters and modulations can be controlled by the mythical grid. In play mode, the 64 pads can be set to a wide variety of scales and intervals. There's aftertouch, and additional controller data is generated depending on where you hit and hold the pads. These pads don't give much tactile feedback and although there are multiple levels of brightness, I would have preferred a multi-color approach.

Things get even more complex when entering grid mode. A pattern length of up to 8 bars, swing, and a powerful parameter lock automation system. Over 100 parameters can be stored, so it's more or less one patch per step, which can be copy-pasted. The randomizer works great. You can change sequencer direction and parameter locks will be deactivated in play mode.

## Quirks, Limitations, and Discontinuation

MIDI implementation can be odd at times. Many essential parameters are hidden in the menus. Faders and knobs have some wobbliness to them, and although I deeply appreciate the MIDI trio, the single mono output feels like a limitation. Medusa was discontinued in 2021. According to Polyend, I got the last one they had in stock, and used prices seem reasonable given the huge feature set of the instrument.

Medusa appears to be the best of both worlds. How did it arouse so much controversy that even Ben Jordan felt the need to make a dedicated video about it? You have already heard Medusa in today's intro tune. That's pretty solid. The grid can be intimidating. Let's limit ourselves to the synth and control the section in the first gem.

## First Music Demo: Synth Section

I usually know how to dial in a bass tone, but I'm not entirely satisfied with this. All the ingredients are there, but I was hoping for a little more Moog-ish beefiness. The brassy tones work great, and the controller pads are super expressive when you put in a little practice time.

## Second Music Demo: Sequencer & P-Locks

To give the parameter locks of the grid a go.

That's more like it. The strange mix of analog and digital sounds works well in the busy arrangement and the sequencer is easy to use once you make sense of the overall concept. I lost track of what's going on after programming a few parameter locks, though.

## Third Music Demo: Processed with Effects

Medusa really shines when combined with external effects. Let's put it through the DAW ringer in this speculative fiction fantasy electro old school base music.

## Final Verdict

Verdict: Medusa is a strange beast. The idea of combining Polyend's digital high-tech with the analog sound of a Dreadbox classic like the Erebus is great, but regardless of how much I like the philosophies of both manufacturers, the two cerebral hemispheres of the instrument don't seem to communicate flawlessly. Sure, the raw oscillator tones, the versatile sequencer, the countless modulation options, and endless list of innovative features turn it into a powerful toolbox for experienced sound designers, but as soon as I tried to dial in more conventional tones, I was missing the sophistication, punch and meatiness I would have expected from an instrument of Medusa's heritage.

However, I'm warming to the idea of collaborations between synth manufacturers. The world totally needs an Arturia/1010music SampleBrute, a life-changing psychedelic SOMA/Hydrasynth experience, and maybe Korg can show Roland how to conveniently insert groove boxes into your... oh, never mind. Thanks for watching and see you next time.

## Outro

Hey guys, I hope you enjoyed the episode. Feel free to like, subscribe, become a patron, and leave a comment. What other kind of gear you would like to see and hear on the show?
